units.title: Names, identity, mutability, copying and hashability
outcomes: Explain name binding, identity and equality using a novel nested-object example, and state when CPython may reuse an immutable object.
Predict visible mutations for aliases, shallow copies and deep copies of a nested structure.
State the dictionary and set key contract, including why a tuple holding a list is unhashable and why NaN lookups fail.
units.why: Almost every silent data bug is shared mutable state. This unit makes aliasing visible before frameworks add more of it.

next.note: Follow mutation across call boundaries and mutable defaults.
Connect aliasing to object lifetimes and weak references.

study.title: Default equality and hashing
study.locator: `object.__eq__` and `object.__hash__`: default identity equality; defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` removes hashing

focus: Assignment binds a name to an object. `is` tests identity and `==` tests value; CPython reuses small immutable objects, but the reference says reuse may or may not happen, so never branch on it.
Two names can own one mutable object. A shallow copy shares every nested object; only a deep copy duplicates them. Copying an immutable such as a `tuple` or `str` may return the same object.
A key must stay hashable and equal for its lifetime in the container. A `tuple` is hashable only when all its items are; NaN never equals itself, so a fresh NaN misses a stored NaN key.
The cookbook says tuples are hashable because they are immutable. That shortcut is wrong for tuples that hold mutables; `hash((1, [2]))` raises `TypeError`.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, predict `a`, `c` and `d` after `a = [[0]]`; `b = a`; `c = copy.copy(a)`; `d = copy.deepcopy(a)`; `b[0].append(1)`. Then quote the measured copy costs: shallow about 3 us and deep about 1.4 ms per copy of a 2000 by 10 nested list on CPython 3.14.4 default build, 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K, `timeit.repeat` best of 5.
traps: Comparing values with `is`. Constant folding makes `257 is 257` true inside one compilation unit, and CPython warns (`SyntaxWarning`) on `is` with a literal, so `is` proves nothing about equality.
`dict.fromkeys(keys, [])` shares one list across all keys; appending through one key shows up under every key.
Reading `d[float('nan')]` after storing under another NaN. Lookup needs equality with the stored key, and NaN never equals NaN.

selfTest.q: After `a = [1, [2]]`; `b = a`; `c = copy.copy(a)`; `b.append(3)`; `b[1].append(4)`, what are `a` and `c`?
selfTest.a: `a` is `[1, [2, 4], 3]` because `b` names the same list. `c` is `[1, [2, 4]]`: its outer list was copied before the append, but it shares the inner list.

selfTest.q: Why does `hash((1, 2))` work while `hash((1, [2]))` raises `TypeError`?
selfTest.a: Tuple hashing needs every item hashable. A `list` is unhashable, so the `tuple` is unhashable despite being immutable.

selfTest.q: `d = {}`; `k = float('nan')`; `d[k] = 1`. Why does `d[float('nan')]` raise `KeyError`?
selfTest.a: Lookup compares by hash then equality, and NaN never equals NaN, so the fresh key never matches the stored one.

selfTest.q: Give a case where `x is y` holds but `x == y` is `False`.
selfTest.a: `x = y = float('nan')`. Identity holds and equality is `False`. Apart from pathological `__eq__` definitions, identity implies equality.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: diagnosing and fixing the seeded aliasing defect with a regression test.
units.stopWhen: You predict the alias, copy and NaN cases without running them, and your copy-cost numbers match a fresh `timeit` run.

fit.note: The cookbook copying and collection sections plus Data model 3.1 cover all three topics at explain depth, with copy costs measured locally; the section mini-project supplies the aliasing practice.

study.title: Closures
study.locator: The Closures lesson and Exercise: Closures; predict each output before checking

focus: Defaults evaluate once at function definition time. The `None` sentinel plus a fresh list inside the body is the standard fix.
Arguments pass by assignment: rebinding a parameter is invisible to the caller, while mutating a mutable argument is visible.
Closures capture variables, not values. Loop closures share the final value; a default argument binds the current one.
A name bound anywhere in a block is local everywhere in it. Reading it before assignment raises `UnboundLocalError`; `global` and `nonlocal` redirect the binding.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `make_funcs` returning three closures over `range(3)` so each returns its own index, plus a `nonlocal` counter starting at 0. State that the naive loop version returns `[2, 2, 2]` on CPython 3.14.4.
traps: Believing closures snapshot values. They read the live cell at call time.
Using `+=` on a `global` without a `global` statement. Augmented assignment binds, so the name goes local and the read fails.
Treating every parameter before `*` as positional-only. Only parameters before `/` are; `c` in `def g(a, b, /, c, *, d)` still accepts keywords.

selfTest.q: `def f(x, acc=[]): acc.append(x); return acc`. What do `f(1)` and `f(2)` return, and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: `f(1)` is `[1]` and `f(2)` is `[1, 2]`: one list is shared across calls. Default to `None` and build a fresh list in the body.

selfTest.q: What does `[fn() for fn in [lambda: i for i in range(3)]]` give, and why?
selfTest.a: `[2, 2, 2]`. Each closure reads the same cell `i`, which holds 2 after the loop.

selfTest.q: `x = 10` at module level. `def f(): print(x); x = 1`. What does `f()` do?
selfTest.a: It raises `UnboundLocalError`. The assignment makes `x` local for the whole block, so the print reads an unbound local.

selfTest.q: In `def g(a, b, /, c, *, d)`, which parameters can be passed by keyword?
selfTest.a: `c` and `d`. `a` and `b` are positional-only and raise `TypeError` when passed by keyword.

study.title: Data Classes
study.locator: The Data Classes lesson and Exercise: Data Classes after the cookbook pass

focus: Lookup order is data descriptors, then the instance dictionary, then non-data descriptors and class attributes. Implicit dunder calls use the type only, so an instance `__len__` attribute never changes `len(obj)`.
`object.__eq__` is identity by default. Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to `None` and the instances become unhashable.
Dataclass mutable defaults raise `ValueError` at class creation; `field(default_factory=list)` gives each instance its own list.
The cookbook writes `Config(frozen=True)`. That call is wrong and raises `TypeError`; `frozen` belongs on the decorator as `@dataclass(frozen=True)`.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a frozen slotted dataclass with two validated fields, `__post_init__` checks, an `asdict` round trip and a `replace()` change. State why its instances are hashable and which line breaks if `frozen` is removed.
traps: Setting an instance `__len__` to change `len()`. Implicit lookup skips the instance dictionary.
Expecting `<` on a default dataclass to work. `order` defaults to `False`, so `P(1) < P(2)` raises `TypeError`.
Sharing state through a plain `list` default. The decorator rejects it with `ValueError`; read that error as protection.

selfTest.q: A data descriptor, an instance entry and a plain class attribute all define `x`. Which does `obj.x` return?
selfTest.a: The data descriptor wins. Instance lookup only beats non-data descriptors and plain class attributes.

selfTest.q: A class defines `__eq__` but no `__hash__`. What does `hash(instance)` do?
selfTest.a: It raises `TypeError`. Defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to `None` unless `__hash__` is also defined.

selfTest.q: What happens at class creation for `tags: list = []` inside `@dataclass`, and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: `ValueError`: mutable default is not allowed. Use `tags: list = field(default_factory=list)`.

selfTest.q: Why does removing `frozen=True` from a hashed dataclass break set membership?
selfTest.a: Instances become unhashable because `eq` without `frozen` sets `__hash__` to `None`. Mutable hashed instances are worse: edits strand them in the wrong bucket.

study.title: Generators
study.locator: The Generators lesson and Exercise: Generators; then the `yield` Statement lesson for `send` and `return` values

focus: An iterable makes fresh iterators; an iterator is consumed once. `iter()` on a `list` gives a new object each time, while a generator is its own single-pass iterator.
Generators suspend at `yield` and resume after it. `send()` delivers a value to the paused `yield` expression; a `return` value becomes `StopIteration.value`; `close()` raises `GeneratorExit` inside.
Raising `StopIteration` inside a generator body is a `RuntimeError` since Python 3.7 by PEP 479; use `return` to stop.
Lazy wins memory only when nothing materializes. One `list()` call in the middle removes the gain; measure peak with `tracemalloc` on the same workload.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement a repeatable `Range` iterable and a single-pass variant; assert the second `list()` pass is full for the first and empty for the second. Then run the eager versus lazy comparison: `list` of 1M squares peaks near 40 MB while the genexpr sum peaks under 1 KiB with equal results, measured with `tracemalloc` on CPython 3.14.4 default build, 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K.
traps: Re-iterating an exhausted generator and expecting fresh data. The second pass is empty with no error.
An accidental `StopIteration` inside a generator body. It surfaces as `RuntimeError`, not a quiet stop.
`itertools.groupby` across unsorted input. It groups consecutive items only; sort first or accept split groups.

selfTest.q: How do you test whether an object is an iterable or an iterator?
selfTest.a: Call `iter()` twice: a `list` gives two distinct working iterators, while a generator returns itself. `list()` on an exhausted generator is `[]`.

selfTest.q: A generator yields 1 then raises `StopIteration('x')`. What does the caller see?
selfTest.a: `RuntimeError` by PEP 479, not `StopIteration`. End a generator with `return`, optionally with a value.

selfTest.q: How does a caller read a value returned by a generator, and how does it send one in?
selfTest.a: `return 'done'` surfaces as `StopIteration.value` on exhaustion. `send(v)` resumes the paused `yield` expression with `v`; prime with `next()` first.

selfTest.q: The lazy pipeline uses the same peak memory as the eager one. What is the first suspect?
selfTest.a: Something materializes: a `list()`, `sorted()`, `len()` or reuse of the data downstream. Find the allocating line with `tracemalloc`.

study.locator: The functools Module lesson: compare `wraps`, `lru_cache` and `partial` behavior after the cookbook pass

focus: A decorator replaces the function object. Without `@wraps` the name, docstring and signature come from the wrapper; with it, `__wrapped__` points back.
A decorator with arguments is three levels: the factory call, then the decorator, then the wrapper. State which level each argument belongs to.
`lru_cache` and cache key on all arguments. Unhashable arguments raise `TypeError`; an unbounded cache grows one entry per distinct call.
Wrappers must forward `*args` and `**kwargs` untouched, including `self` for methods; returning the inner result keeps the return contract.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `retry(times)` that preserves `__name__` and reruns on `ValueError`, and show three attempts ending in success plus `lru_cache` raising `TypeError` on a `list` argument (both verified on CPython 3.14.4).
traps: Forgetting `@wraps` on a wrapper. Test ids and help show wrapper and failures get harder to trace.
Writing `@retry` without the factory call. The function lands in the `times` parameter, the name is bound to the inner decorator, and the first call wraps its argument instead of running.
Caching a function of large or unhashable inputs. Memory grows silently or the first call raises TypeError.

selfTest.q: What breaks when `@wraps` is missing from a wrapper?
selfTest.a: `__name__`, `__doc__` and the signature come from the wrapper, and `__wrapped__` is absent. Debuggers, help and pytest ids show wrapper.

selfTest.q: Why does a cached function fail on `f([1, 2])`?
selfTest.a: Cache keys need hashing and `list` is unhashable, so the call raises `TypeError` before the body runs.

selfTest.q: Sketch the three levels of `@retry(3)` and what each receives.
selfTest.a: `retry(3)` returns the decorator; the decorator receives the function; the wrapper receives the call arguments and loops.

selfTest.q: A timed decorator swallows the return value. Which contract breaks, and what is the one-line fix?
selfTest.a: Callers get `None` instead of the result. Return `fn(*args, **kwargs)` from the wrapper, through `try`/`finally` for timing.

study.title: Context Managers
study.locator: The Context Managers lesson and Exercise: Context Managers; then the `with` Statement lesson

focus: Exceptions in the `with` body are thrown into the `@contextmanager` generator at the `yield` point; the `finally` clause still runs before propagation.
`__exit__` returning true suppresses; anything falsy re-raises. Swallowing by accident hides the failure the caller must see.
`raise New from e` keeps the cause; `from None` hides context deliberately. A bare `raise` re-raises the same exception with its traceback.
`ExceptionGroup` splits across `except*` clauses since Python 3.11: handled members are removed and the rest keeps propagating.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a `@contextmanager` owning a temp file plus a two-level `ConfigError` hierarchy with a CLI exit-code map. Prove the file closes on an inner `ValueError` and that the mapped error keeps its `__cause__`.
traps: A bare `except`: swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`. Catch `Exception` at broadest, and re-raise what you do not handle.
An exception raised in `finally` or in `__exit__` replaces the in-flight one. Keep cleanup paths total and narrow.
Catching an `ExceptionGroup` with `except` instead of `except*`. Plain `except` matches the whole group object and never the members.

selfTest.q: Where does an exception raised in a `with` body surface inside a `@contextmanager` generator?
selfTest.a: At the `yield` point, as if the `yield` raised it. `try`/`finally` around the `yield` runs cleanup, then the exception propagates unless caught.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between `raise E from e`, `raise E from None` and bare `raise`?
selfTest.a: `from e` sets `__cause__` and shows both tracebacks; `from None` suppresses the context; bare `raise` re-raises the active exception unchanged.

selfTest.q: `except* ValueError` handles half an `ExceptionGroup`. What happens to the rest?
selfTest.a: The remaining members propagate as a group. `except*` subtracts matches; unmatched members keep traveling.

selfTest.q: When does the `else` clause of `try` run, and what is it for?
selfTest.a: Only when no exception occurred. It separates code that must not be protected from the risky block, so its own failures stay distinct.

focus: Annotations are lazily evaluated since 3.14 by PEP 649: `def f(x: 1/0)` defines fine and fails only when `__annotations__` is read. `get_type_hints` evaluates them in the right scope.
PEP 695 in 3.12 puts type parameters in brackets: `def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T`. Read old `TypeVar` code; write the new syntax.
A `Protocol` defines structure, not lineage. `isinstance` against a non-`runtime_checkable` `Protocol` raises `TypeError`; a `runtime_checkable` check tests member presence only.
Narrowing proves a type at a point: `isinstance` branches plus `assert_type` as the checkable claim. `isinstance` with a parameterized generic raises `TypeError`.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, type a generic `first()` plus a small `Protocol` and a narrowing function over `int | str`; run mypy 2.4.0 clean. Show that `def f(x: 1/0)` defines without error on 3.14 and raises only on annotation access.
traps: Checking with `isinstance(x, list[int])`. Parameterized generics are not valid `isinstance` targets.
Treating a `runtime_checkable` `Protocol` as a full interface check. It verifies member presence, never signatures or semantics.
Assuming annotations run at `def` time. On 3.14 a `ZeroDivisionError` inside an annotation waits until someone reads it, which delays import-time failures.

selfTest.q: `def f(x: 1/0) -> None: pass` runs without error on 3.14. When does it fail, and which PEP changed this?
selfTest.a: It fails when `__annotations__` is read, through the lazy `__annotate__` hook. PEP 649 made annotations lazily evaluated in 3.14.

selfTest.q: What does `isinstance([], list[int])` do, and what should you write instead?
selfTest.a: It raises `TypeError`: parameterized generics are not valid `isinstance` targets. Check `isinstance(x, list)` and narrow items separately, or use `assert_type` for the static claim.

selfTest.q: `class P(Protocol): def m(self) -> int`. What does `isinstance(obj, P)` do without `@runtime_checkable`?
selfTest.a: It raises `TypeError`. Structural checks need `@runtime_checkable`, which then checks member presence only.

selfTest.q: Rewrite `class Box(Generic[T])` with 3.12 syntax and state the minimum version.
selfTest.a: `class Box[T]: ...` needs Python 3.12 or later by PEP 695.

focus: Importing executes the module once per process and caches it in `sys.modules`. A second import binds the same object; `reload()` re-executes but old objects keep old classes.

`sys.path[0]` differs by launch: a script prepends its own directory while `-m` prepends the current directory. The same file run as a script and imported as a module executes twice, as `__main__` and under its real name.
Regular packages need `__init__.py`; namespace packages merge path portions without one. Relative imports need package context and fail in bare scripts.
Editable installs register the project in the environment; path hacks only fake it. The passing test is a clean-environment install with no `sys.path` edits.
units.reproduce: From a blank directory, create a src-layout package named `atlas_demo` with an `add()` function and an `atlas-demo` entry point; build the sdist and wheel; install the wheel in a clean environment and run the entry point to print 5 with no `sys.path` edits.
traps: Running tests from the package directory and importing the local tree by accident. The clean-environment install test exists to catch exactly this.
Two copies of one module: tests `import pkg.mod` while a script already ran it as `__main__`. State lives in two places and singletons split.
Using `pip freeze` for requirements. It captures the whole environment; record direct dependencies and verify with the clean install.

selfTest.q: `import pkg.mod` runs twice in one process. How many executions happen, and how do you prove it?
selfTest.a: One. The second import rebinds from `sys.modules`; the new name is `sys.modules['pkg.mod']`.

selfTest.q: Why does `python sub/show.py` differ from `python -m sub.show` in `sys.path[0]`?
selfTest.a: The script prepends its own directory; `-m` prepends the current directory. Imports resolve differently from each.

selfTest.q: A script imports its sibling fine but fails after moving to a `src` layout. What changed?
selfTest.a: The sibling is no longer on `sys.path` and implicit siblings are gone. Install the package or run from a layout that puts `src` on the path; do not hand-edit `sys.path` as the fix.

selfTest.q: What distinguishes an editable install from a `PYTHONPATH` hack?
selfTest.a: The editable install registers package metadata and entry points in the environment; `PYTHONPATH` only shadows imports and leaves every other machine broken.

study.title: The cycle collector
study.locator: `collect`, `get_count`, `get_threshold`, `garbage` and `disable`/`enable`
study.depth: The generations changed within 3.14: 3.14.0 to 3.14.4 run an incremental collector (`gc.get_threshold()` reads `(2000, 10, 0)` on 3.14.4), and the docs record that 3.14.5 restores the three 3.13 generations. Read `gc.get_threshold()` on your interpreter before reasoning about generations.

study.title: Weak references
study.locator: Weak-reference objects with callbacks; which types refuse weakrefs; the `WeakValueDictionary` pattern

study.title: Finding leaks
study.locator: Profiling CPU and Memory: Finding leaks (`gc.collect`, `gc.garbage`) with the refcounting one-liner; `tracemalloc` above it for sizing

focus: CPython frees by refcount immediately and collects cycles later. A self-referencing object with `__del__` is still collected since Python 3.4 by PEP 442.

`sys.getrefcount` counts its own argument, and CPython 3.14 borrows references when it loads locals, so one fresh object reads 2 at module level and 1 inside a function. The docs promise nothing beyond 0 or 1; compare readings taken in one context, never absolutes.

`weakref.ref` fails on `list` and `dict` instances (subclasses can opt in), on `tuple` and `int`, and on slotted classes without `__weakref__`; sets and frozensets support it. Caches want `WeakValueDictionary`, not manual callback books.
`gc.garbage` holds objects the collector refused; an empty list after `gc.collect()` proves the run happened, not that nothing leaked.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, build a two-object cycle with a `__del__` method and a `weakref` callback, delete both names, and, with `gc.disable()` first, show that nothing runs until `gc.collect()`, which fires the callback and both `__del__` methods. Then show `sys.getrefcount` on a fresh object reads 2 at module level and 1 inside a function on CPython 3.14.4.
traps: Depending on `__del__` timing. Collection order is unspecified, so close resources explicitly.
Caching instances in a plain `dict`. The cache owns them forever; `WeakValueDictionary` or explicit eviction bounds it.
Reading `gc.garbage` as the leak list. It holds objects the collector refused; ordinary leaks never appear there.

selfTest.q: `a = []`; `b = [a]`; `a.append(b)`; `del a, b`. When is the memory freed?
selfTest.a: At the next cycle collection, not at `del`. Refcounts stay positive through the cycle; `gc.collect()` reclaims both.

selfTest.q: `sys.getrefcount(x)` reads 2 for a fresh object at module level but 1 inside a function. Why?
selfTest.a: The argument adds a temporary reference, but 3.14 loads locals as borrowed references, so the function call adds none. Only deltas taken in the same context mean anything.

selfTest.q: `weakref.ref([1, 2, 3])` raises `TypeError`. Why?
selfTest.a: `list` does not support weak references (a subclass of `list` does). Hold weakref-able objects instead, or use `WeakValueDictionary` for caches.

selfTest.q: A slotted class cannot be weak-referenced. What is missing?
selfTest.a: `__weakref__` in `__slots__`. Without that slot the type has no weak-reference support.
